title: Fraction Converter
description: Count the zeros of the denominator and slide the point into place, write zeros in front of a short numerator, and turn a decimal back into a fraction in lowest terms.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit. With navDots the dots are controls in AI mode too: a tap on a dot starts that phase.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; Hint, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 640. One rounded card holding the key at its top right (Answer, Close, Enter, Next, or the Yes / No keys; no question bar), the working area (the whole card until Answer is tapped) and the answer drawer that slides in from the right; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 652 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it (y 656 to 892, the question and every line, printed), one small dot per phase at the right.

zones.layout: board, key only: no question bar, only its key at the right end of the top row (the question is on the bubble); the working area is the whole card (64, 108, 1472 x 520) until the child taps Answer, when the answer drawer (as tall as the working area, the key on its top row reading Close) slides in from the right
zones.controls: circles r 28 at cx 1388, 1460, 1532, cy 40: Hint (data-control again), sound, restart; 72-unit finger boxes
zones.dots: one small dot per phase at the footer's right (72-unit finger boxes, centred on the bubble), no text; in user AND AI mode each is a button (data-control phase-dot, data-phase k) that starts its phase

stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box on the stage. The score leaves on finished and onComplete and is shown once, as stars on the summary page.

writeup.why: Convert a fraction with a denominator of 10, 100 or 1000, or one that can be brought to it, into a decimal, and convert a decimal into a fraction in lowest terms.
writeup.look: A fraction card and a row of digit cards, a Zeros counter and a Count button under them, a Times both slider on the third phase and a Factors row on the last.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Fraction Converter' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x sixty-four, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many digits have been counted from the right, one for each digit lit. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x sixty-four, y 202. The fraction card stands at x 110, y 240, 180 by 200, its numerator deep blue above the bar and its denominator in ink below. The digit cards run to its right from x 360 at y 280, each 80 across, one digit to a card, with room for grey zero cards to slide in at the front. The Zeros counter sits under the fraction card at y 470 and the Count button beside it at x 360. When the point drops it sits large and near-black between two cards, and the decimal is written green at y 400 under the row. The Times both slider runs along y 560 from x 110 to x 700, its handle showing the number both terms are multiplied by. On the last phase the Factors row runs along y 640, one chip for each common factor, the HCF lit amber. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across with a point key and a fraction bar key, for setting a fraction with a denominator up to 1000 or a decimal with up to three places, or for typing an answer into the slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the tools of this chapter share them. A decimal or fraction the question gives is deep blue, with the shaded parts that show it. The result the working reaches, a decimal, a fraction, a sum, a difference or what is left, is green, with its shaded parts. Ten of one place traded for one of the next, a carry in adding or a trade in taking away, is vermilion. A zero written after the point to line decimals up is violet, and so is the point written after a whole number before those zeros. The part taken away, used or poured out is rose. The digit, place or step being worked on now, and the first place where two decimals differ, are amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey, and nothing else on the stage is ever grey. An unshaded part stays warm white inside its near-black outline, the decimal point is near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label, Given, Answer, Carry, Trade, Added zero, Taken away, Left or Place holder, before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last fraction and its decimal side by side, the counted digits lit under the point.

phases.win: the point drops in front of the four, a grey 0 fills the ones place, and 0.43 is written in green
phases.does: counts the two zeros, taps Count, and watches two digits light and the point drop before them
phases.goal: the zeros of 10, 100 or 1000 say how many digits come after the point
phases.says: Count the zeros at the bottom. That many digits go after the point.
phases.check: Away from the screen: how many digits come after the point in a number of hundredths?
phases.feels: the point dropping into place after the count
phases.hands: Lay number cards for a numerator in a row, and a card for 10, 100 or 1000 under them. Count the zeros on the bottom card, count that many cards from the right, and put the dot card before them.
phases.tries: First rung: count the zeros at the bottom. Second rung: count that many digits from the right. Third rung: the same task with a denominator of 10, before the longer denominators return.

wrong.why: counting from the right ends on the left of those digits, and it is easy to stop on the wrong side
wrong.move: puts the point after the counted digits instead of before them
wrong.screen: the counted digits light amber and the point slides to their left edge, with the child's own row kept above

wrong.why: all the digits of the bottom number are right there
wrong.move: counts the digits of the denominator instead of its zeros
wrong.screen: the one in front of the zeros fades to half strength and the zeros light one by one, the counter ticking with each

phases.screen: 43/100 on the fraction card, its digits 4 and 3 on cards, and the Zeros counter at nothing
phases.soWhat: the zeros of 10, 100 or 1000 say how many digits come after the point

phases.win: the row reads 004 with the point before it and a 0 in the ones place, and 0.004 is written in green
phases.does: counts three zeros, taps Count, and watches two grey zero cards slide in front of the four
phases.goal: a short numerator gets zeros in front of it, and a 0 in the ones place
phases.says: Three places are needed, but there is only one digit. What fills the gap?
phases.check: Away from the screen: a numerator has one digit and the denominator has three zeros. How many zeros go in front?
phases.feels: zeros sliding in to fill a gap nobody saw
phases.hands: Lay a one-digit numerator over the 1000 card. Count three places from the right, add zero cards in front until there are enough, put the dot card before them and a zero card in the ones place.
phases.tries: First rung: count the zeros at the bottom. Second rung: count the digits on top. Third rung: the same task with a denominator of 100, before 1000 returns.

wrong.why: the numerator's digit is the only thing there to count
wrong.move: puts the point straight before the one digit, with no zeros in front
wrong.screen: the count runs on past the digit, each missing place lighting amber and filling with a grey zero card

wrong.why: nothing is left to go there, so it seems fine to leave it bare
wrong.move: leaves the ones place empty before the point
wrong.screen: the ones place outlines itself and a grey 0 drops into it, the point staying where it was

phases.screen: 4/1000 on the card and a single digit card, the Zeros counter at nothing
phases.soWhat: a short numerator gets zeros in front of it, and a 0 in the ones place

phases.win: the slider settles at five, the card reads 15/100, and 0.15 is written in green
phases.does: drags the slider until the denominator lands on 100, then taps Count
phases.goal: a denominator that goes exactly into 10, 100 or 1000 is multiplied up to it first, and 1/3 never gets there
phases.says: The count only works on ten, a hundred or a thousand. Can you reach one?
phases.check: Away from the screen: can one quarter be written with a denominator of a hundred? Can one third?
phases.feels: the slider clicking into place on a denominator of a hundred
phases.hands: Write a fraction whose denominator is not 10, 100 or 1000. Multiply both terms by the same number until the denominator is 10, 100 or 1000, then count the zeros. Try it with one third and see what happens.
phases.tries: First rung: ask whether the denominator goes into 10 exactly. Second rung: try 100. Third rung: the same task with a denominator of 5, before larger denominators return.

wrong.why: it has a zero, so the counting rule looks as if it fits
wrong.move: counts the one zero of a denominator that only ends in zero
wrong.screen: the Count button stays off and pulses once, and the slider handle lights amber to show where to start

wrong.why: the bottom number is the one that has to change
wrong.move: multiplies only the denominator up to 100
wrong.screen: the card built that way is set beside the first one with both shaded on a strip, and the two shaded runs end in different places

phases.screen: 3/20 on the card, the Count button off, and the Times both slider at one
phases.soWhat: a denominator that goes exactly into 10, 100 or 1000 is multiplied up to it first, and 1/3 never gets there

phases.win: 275/100 appears, the HCF twenty-five lights amber, and the card settles on 11/4
phases.does: taps Back, reads the fraction, fills the Factors row and divides both terms by the HCF
phases.goal: a decimal goes over 1 with a zero for each digit after the point, then is divided by the HCF
phases.says: Count the digits after the point. Then find the biggest factor both terms share.
phases.check: Away from the screen: a decimal has two digits after the point. What is the denominator before you simplify?
phases.feels: a long fraction shrinking to its smallest form in one step
phases.hands: Write a decimal on a slip. Write its digits without the point over 1 and a zero for each digit after the point. List the factors both terms share and divide both by the largest.
phases.tries: First rung: count the digits after the point. Second rung: write the fraction over 10, 100 or 1000. Third rung: the same task with one digit after the point, before longer decimals return.

wrong.why: the whole number digits and the digits after the point get mixed up
wrong.move: writes one zero too few in the denominator
wrong.screen: the digits after the point light amber one by one, and a zero appears on the denominator for each

wrong.why: the fraction is already right, so it feels finished
wrong.screen: the Factors row lights the factor the two terms still share, and the card waits beside the child's fraction

phases.screen: 2.75 on the digit cards and the Back button lit
phases.soWhat: a decimal goes over 1 with a zero for each digit after the point, then is divided by the HCF

writeup.delight: On the second phase, when the count runs past the numerator's last digit, grey zero cards slide in from the left one after another with a soft tick each, and the point drops into place in front of them.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with the fraction card and its digit cards in place and no point yet. On the first phase the Zeros counter stands at nothing. On the second the numerator has fewer digits than the denominator has zeros. On the third the Count button is switched off and the Times both slider rests at one. On the fourth a decimal sits on the digit cards with the Back button lit. One thing moves, once: the Zeros counter, the slider handle or the Back button gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: A fraction with a denominator up to 1000 or a decimal with up to three places, of the child's own, both ways, with the Times both slider and the Factors row. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on counting the zeros, zeros in front, reaching 10, 100 or 1000, and decimals back to fractions.
voiceLines: A fraction, and a row of digit cards waiting for a point.
Count the zeros at the bottom. That many digits go after the point.
Three places are needed, but there is only one digit. What fills the gap?
The count only works on ten, a hundred or a thousand. Can you reach one?
Count the digits after the point. Then find the biggest factor both terms share.
A new fraction. Look at the bottom number first.
Free play. Pick your own fraction or decimal, and turn it either way.
Count the zeros at the bottom again, then count that many digits.
The zeros told you where the point goes, every time.

observations.why: tenths take one place, hundredths two and thousandths three.
observations.soWhat: the zeros of 10, 100 or 1000 say how many digits come after the point.
observations.observe: The number of zeros at the bottom always matched the number of digits after the point.

observations.why: every place after the point needs a digit, even an empty one.
observations.soWhat: a short numerator gets zeros in front of it, and a 0 in the ones place.
observations.observe: Grey zero cards slid in when the numerator ran out of digits.

observations.why: only a denominator that goes exactly into 10, 100 or 1000 can be multiplied up to one of them.
observations.soWhat: make the denominator 10, 100 or 1000 itself before counting zeros; 1/3 has no such form.
observations.observe: The slider settled for some denominators and ran to its end for others.

observations.why: the HCF is the largest factor the two terms share.
observations.soWhat: a decimal goes over 10, 100 or 1000 and then is divided by the HCF for lowest terms.
observations.observe: Dividing by the lit factor left a fraction nothing more would divide.

phases.screen: 43/100 on the fraction card, its digits 4 and 3 on cards, and the Zeros counter at nothing
phases.win: the point drops in front of the four, a grey 0 fills the ones place, and 0.43 is written in green
phases.traceback: The zeros light one by one, as many digits light from the right, the point drops before them, a 0 fills the ones place and the decimal is written green.
ladder: 100 has two zeros, so how many digits go after the point?
Count the zeros of 100 before you place the point.
This time count the zeros of 1,000, not of 100.
Count that many digits from the right of the top number.
The point goes just before those digits, and 0 goes in front of it.

phases.screen: 4/1000 on the card and a single digit card, the Zeros counter at nothing
phases.win: the row reads 004 with the point before it and a 0 in the ones place, and 0.004 is written in green
phases.traceback: The count runs past the top number into empty places, grey zero cards slide into them, the point drops, the whole number or a 0 fills the ones place and the decimal is written green.
ladder: The 7 fills one place, so what goes in the other two?
Two places but one digit: what fills the gap?
41 fills two of the three places, so which place is empty?
Count the digits on top, and give each empty place a zero.
The zeros go between the point and the digits, never at the end.

phases.screen: 3/20 on the card, the Count button off, and the Times both slider at one
phases.win: the slider settles at five, the card reads 15/100, and 0.15 is written in green
phases.traceback: Count stays off and rings once, the slider steps until the bottom lands on 100, the zeros are counted and the point drops; for one sixth the slider runs to its end and 10, 100 and 1,000 shared by 6 each leave 4.
ladder: 20 is not 10, 100 or 1,000, so slide to multiply both terms.
Multiply the top by the same number as the bottom.
Slide all the way along: does the bottom ever land on 10, 100 or 1,000?
Try 100: which number times the bottom makes 100?
Think of one fifth: times 2 it is two tenths, which is 0.2.

phases.screen: 2.75 on the digit cards and the Back button lit
phases.win: 275/100 appears, the HCF twenty-five lights amber, and the card settles on 11/4
phases.traceback: The digits after the point light one by one with a zero on the denominator for each, the common factors fill with the HCF lit, and both terms are divided by it to lowest terms, in green.
ladder: 4.35 is 435 hundredths, so divide both terms by their HCF.
One digit after the point means 10 at the bottom: what do 8 and 10 share?
1205 hundredths is equal, but is it as small as it gets?
Find the biggest number that goes into both terms.
Tap Factors, then divide the top and the bottom by the biggest one.
Which number times 6 gives 10, 100 or 1,000?
Share 10, 100 and 1,000 by 6: does any of them leave nothing over?

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: The zeros light one by one, as many digits light from the right, the point drops before them, a 0 fills the ones place and the decimal is written green.
Phase 2: The count runs past the top number into empty places, grey zero cards slide into them, the point drops, the whole number or a 0 fills the ones place and the decimal is written green.

Phase 3: Count stays off and rings once, the slider steps until the bottom lands on 100, the zeros are counted and the point drops; for one sixth the slider runs to its end and 10, 100 and 1,000 shared by 6 each leave 4.
Phase 4: The digits after the point light one by one with a zero on the denominator for each, the common factors fill with the HCF lit, and both terms are divided by it to lowest terms, in green.

voice.opening: A fraction, and a row of digit cards waiting for a point.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play: tap a card and type your own fraction or decimal.
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs, shown at once UNDER the pinned instruction and kept until the child acts again
voice.onFinish: The zeros told you where the point goes, every time.
voice.rules: Silent: nothing is spoken (no device speech, no recorded clips, no Tap to start cover). The speech bubble is the guide: every instruction and hint is one printed page, numbers as words. The lesson is action-driven in every mode: a guide step's instruction stays until the child does the act it names; a wrong act shows that step's hint under the pinned instruction, a wrong answer the next rung of its ladder, and the hint stays unchanged until the child acts again; a right answer's next question, a phase's next phase and the summary's rows follow by themselves after a short celebration. The header's Hint key shows the step's hint or the next rung on demand. What is heard is sound effects (Web Audio), switched by the sound button, on in every mode. In classroom mode nothing waits for a tap except the pieces of a long line (the blinking arrow; a tap, Enter, Space, ArrowRight or PageDown on the bubble shows the next piece), and a tap on the bubble when nothing waits is the teacher's skip.

guide.playsOn: guide steps on phase 1, 2, 3, 4: the phase opens on its first instruction and waits for the child's act (getState guideStep, guideSteps, guideOn); the agent's check() performs the current step; the last act opens the first question. Other phases open on their printed teach lines, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

toolQuestions.source: props.questions ?? props.additionalProps?.questions is read; the authored rows below keep their stage (fitHost returns null).

question.en: Write the fraction on the card as a decimal.
Do the same for this card.
Count first, then write this card as a decimal.
Write the number on the card as a decimal.
Now this card: write its fraction as a decimal.

items.planAnswer: 0.06. 100 has two zeros, so a zero goes in front of the 6

question.en: Mind the gap, then write this card as a decimal.

items.planAnswer: 3.041. 1000 has three zeros, so a zero goes in front of 41

question.en: Write the card's fraction as a decimal.
Find the decimal for this new card.

items.planQuestion: Can 1/6 be written with a denominator of 10, 100 or 1000? Explain.

question.en: Can one sixth be written with a denominator of 10, 100 or 1,000?

items.planAnswer: No. 6 does not go exactly into 10, 100 or 1000, so 1/6 has no such form

items.planQuestion: Write 4.35 as a fraction in lowest terms.

question.en: Write 4.35 as a fraction in lowest terms.

items.planQuestion: Write 0.8 as a fraction in lowest terms.

question.en: Now turn 0.8 into a fraction in lowest terms.

items.planAnswer: 4/5. 0.8 = 8/10, and dividing both terms by their HCF, 2, gives 4/5

items.planQuestion: Write 12.05 as a fraction in lowest terms.

question.en: Watch the zero after the point, and give 12.05 as a fraction in lowest terms.

items.planAnswer: 241/20. 12.05 = 1205/100, and dividing both terms by their HCF, 5, gives 241/20

scoring.wrong: costs nothing, never marked, counted only for first try accuracy
scoring.stars: one for finishing, two at sixty per cent right first time, three at ninety; hidden with the first-try line by showScore false
scoring.phaseMount: a mount scores every phase it plays, from its phase to the last (+5 a question; phases of 3, 3, 3, 3 questions)
scoring.finishCard: stars and the Right first time line under the phase rows on the summary page

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 4; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 4 to the summary page (a tool with nextKey, runtime r48+: in user mode it waits for the child's blinking Next key instead, after every question and every phase, and the last phase's key opens the summary; AI mode, and a host that mounts one phase without navigableDots, walk on by themselves); finished once, from the summary page.
hostContract.navigableDots: true (or no phase): user mode, the phase dots are controls; otherwise AI mode, the dots show progress and the agent drives window.toolApi.

onProgress.done: questions right so far in this phase

hostContract.emits: every event is dispatched on window and, when framed, posted to window.parent as { type: 'event', name, detail }
